extracted.intended_audience: math communicators, educators, aspiring math YouTubers, contest organizers, and self-learners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for producing and selecting high-quality mathematics exposition (especially short videos) and for effective self-teaching in mathematical subjects. Includes criteria for video composition, contest judging/selection, distribution (YouTube nomination), and learner practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide moral/intuition-driven explanations (not only formal steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting proofs or solutions that are merely sequences of steps the viewer can follow; strive to convey why a result should be true — the 'moral understanding' behind it, not just a verifiable chain of steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant contrasts two kinds of proofs: those where "you morally understand why the result should be true" and those where "you can follow the steps" but are left wanting. Good exposition aims for the former by motivating ideas, giving intuition, and showing why approaches arise. Anti-pattern: producing technically correct but unmotivated solutions that leave learners unable to generalize or see the idea's origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach through worked calculations and practice ('putting in the reps')
rubrics_metrics.description: For self-learners, don't skip doing calculations and exercises — these concrete reps solidify intuition and reveal the core mechanisms behind results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant emphasizes that skipping calculations is a common self-learning mistake; doing exercises can reveal why features like a square root create particular behavior. Recommendation: keep a notebook and pencil, actively work through derivations. Anti-pattern: passive reading without solving problems, which often leads to fragile understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an appropriate medium — paper/pencil or interactive notebooks when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the medium that best supports exploration: for deep mathematical digging, paper and pencil remain the right medium; for simulation/experimentation, fluid programming/notebook environments are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant says when diving into math you should "break out some paper and scribble it out." For questions better served by computation, use a notebook or programming interface that minimizes friction. Tradeoff: high production tooling is useful for distribution, but paper remains ideal for initial problem exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim narrow and low-stakes when starting (niche targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating math exposition content, target an unreasonably narrow audience and keep initial ambitions modest rather than trying to chase a maximal audience immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant advises starting with a very niche target so you produce the best possible content for that group and avoid making content "best for no one." Low-stakes beginnings reduce pressure and allow depth. Anti-pattern: launching with the explicit goal of 'making it big' and producing shallow, broad-appeal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and clarity over raw production polish
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall composition (clarity of exposition, structure, intuition) is more important than sheer production quality, though good tooling can help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant notes tooling/production quality is better now and can enable individuals, but selection filters and good composition determine impact. Examples: a well-composed niche video with modest production can outperform a flashy but poorly-structured one. Anti-pattern: prioritizing flashy visuals while neglecting pedagogical structure or motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design content for quick evaluative impressions (contest/judge constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting to competitions or when being reviewed, expect limited judge time (e.g., judges "spend at most 10 minutes on each piece") so craft submissions that make a strong quick impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice based on the math exposition competition: judges had limited time; the selection process relied on surfacing top items into a top-100 pool. Creators should ensure the core idea and value are evident quickly (good opening, clear takeaway). Anti-pattern: long slow builds that don't reveal value in the brief attention window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scalable peer-review (pairwise comparisons) to surface quality
rubrics_metrics.description: For large submission pools, use pairwise rating/dueling comparisons to produce a partial ordering that reliably surfaces the best entries without requiring exhaustive full reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant describes an algorithmic peer-review system feeding pairs of videos to reviewers who pick which is better; this gives a partially ordered list that likely contains the top contenders in the top ~100. Scoring notes: the system doesn't need to be perfect, just high probability to surface the best items. Operational tip: combine with small judging committees for finer evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination stage matters: proxies and co-watch signals drive discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: On platforms like YouTube, the nomination phase (which videos are even fed into recommendation ML) is crucial; proxies (e.g., co-watch graphs) determine which videos get a chance to be recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant explains that full-scale ML ranking over billions of videos is infeasible; systems use proxies to nominate a subset. Co-watch links (people who watch A also watch B) are key. Implication for creators: getting into the nomination pool (via initial reach, peer-review visibility, co-watch relationships) is more important than micro-optimizing later-stage ranking signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create content that reliably teaches something new and is well-presented
rubrics_metrics.description: A video's likelihood of resonating increases if it gives a viewer a clear new takeaway — they "learned something they otherwise didn't know" — and the presentation is satisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant states that if you make something that is good and satisfies viewers, then—if nominated—it will likely be recommended and spread. Scoring/selection heuristic: prioritize clear learning outcomes and crisp presentation. Anti-pattern: content that is vague, has no clear takeaway, or does not respect the viewer's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of tooling can enable creativity but has tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Building your own tools (e.g., Manim) can unlock bespoke visuals and creative freedom but is often inefficient compared to building on existing frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant describes how owning a tool allows you to 'change the tool to make it able to do that' and may be necessary for certain creative directions; but starting with established video tools or After Effects scripting could be more efficient. Consider cost-benefit when choosing to develop custom tooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social & motivational structures are critical for learning uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of explanations is not the main bottleneck — social factors (peer groups, compelling personal projects, respected teachers) drive whether learners actually engage and persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant references research/arguments that educational tech often benefits those already motivated, and suggests interventions that create social incentives (peer groups, projects, respected role models) are far more impactful than simply producing more explanations. Practical tip: pair resources with social/accountability mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize structure and selection incentives matter for participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modest prizes, clear winners, and the promise of exposure can attract high-quality submissions and motivate creators to complete projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant explains the competition used a modest prize pool ($15,000 total; $500 to many honorable mentions) and the existence of winners helped attract participants. The promise of reach (not just money) was important. Anti-pattern: too-big or overly bureaucratic prizes that discourage participation or overcomplicate selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose analogies and interdisciplinary connections to boost creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: For research/problem-solving, broader exposure to analogies across fields increases the chance of creative breakthroughs; 'analogy' acts as a key resource for mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant suggests the equivalent of nitrogen for mathematicians is the number of available analogies — travel, conferences, collaborations, and cross-field exposure increase these analogies. Operational implication: content and curricula that surface cross-disciplinary metaphors improve problem-solving ability.
